claims.text: Adding a minor amount of Ni to a W–Cu composite will generate a transient liquid phase during a 1100–1300 °C hold.
Ni addition and high-temperature processing will form an in-situ interfacial intermetallic layer in W–Cu.
The interfacial reaction layer will enhance wetting between W and Cu.
Enhanced wetting and diffusion bonding caused by the Ni-derived transient liquid phase will eliminate interfacial voids.
The Ni treatment will suppress phase separation commonly associated with conventional W–Cu processing.
Ni-modified W–Cu will have better thermal transport than a vapor-coated W-powder/Cu baseline without Ni.
Ni-modified W–Cu will have greater mechanical strength and durability under irradiation than the vapor-coated baseline.
The resulting W–Cu composite will be void-free and uniformly bonded.
The interfacial product will be a thin, finely dispersed Ni-based or W–Ni/Cu intermetallic layer.
A protective atmosphere during the 1100–1300 °C hold will prevent oxidation.
The intervention is intended for W particles or interconnected W regions embedded in a Cu matrix.
Processing will remain below the melting point of W.
The composite is expected to withstand thermal cycling and irradiation representative of fusion-reactor joints.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and outcome require elimination of voids and a void-free composite, but the falsification rule only requires a significantly reduced void fraction, so a composite retaining measurable voids could pass the stated test despite failing the stronger prediction.
